insight: tiller Session.run/1 is a blocking GenServer.call with the entire recursive loop inside handle_call/3 (session.ex), AND spawn_subagent calls Session.run/1 synchronously (actions.ex). Any async/observability work must change BOTH paths; inverting the session loop alone does not unblock the parent. Codex verified this against source after an initial 30-line estimate that was 3-5x low.

tiller is event-sourced not checkpointed: Tiller.State.log returns [{action,result}] and Tiller.FakeDriver.context takes a list of actions, so a recorded trajectory prefix is already a valid FakeDriver script and state-at-turn-N is Enum.take(log,n). No checkpointer needed. CAVEAT: replaying actions re-executes tools via Actions.eval, so deterministic replay requires injecting the recorded RESULT, not just replaying the action.

In this environment a compression hook lossily rewrites Bash stdout (drops words, collapses prose to telegraphic form). Reading structured content via `cat`/`sed` in Bash corrupts it — gstack skill section templates came back with placeholder blocks replaced by [->LNN] dedup pointers and unreadable prose. Use the Read tool for skill sections, templates, and any doc whose exact wording matters. A subagent reviewing a design doc hit the same class of problem with the Read summarizer and had to verify via sed/cat -A.

seed mcp serve wraps every port envelope as one text content item in the tools/call result; isError mirrors ok=false. Refusals carry error + exit (2 contention, 3 invalid transition, 4 not found, 6 fenced out); an unknown tool is a JSON-RPC -32602 error, not an envelope. task_get returns state at the top level and the card under "card", not under "task" (task is the id).

An open-seed instantiation on the fastcards backend (copy .seed/, set backend = "fastcards", git init + commit, seed init) is enough to drive the real engine with no remote and no credentials. Adding the test actor to [operators].actors lets it promote its own cards so claim paths are reachable.

docs/decisions.active.json rode to main through #10 with its merge conflict markers still in it and sat there unparseable, because nothing in the tree ever read the file. Every check was green throughout. The files most likely to break this way are exactly the ones every branch appends to (decision logs, learning logs, timelines), and those are the files nobody guards because they read as documentation. If it is machine-readable and checked in, something must parse it in CI or it is not checked. Found by accident, when a second merge produced nested markers.

The atom-table regression test asserted on :erlang.system_info(:atom_count), a VM-global counter, from an async: true case. It passed locally and failed CI with twenty atoms of drift from unrelated tests running alongside it. The repair was a stronger assertion, not a looser one: String.to_existing_atom(name) raising, per name, is deterministic, immune to what else runs, and a bigger claim than the count ever made. Reaching for a global proxy is a sign the assertion has not been named precisely.

Two persistence tests passed while proving nothing. A timed kill let the run finish before the kill landed, and kill_mid_run raced the DynamicSupervisor's own restart, tearing down processes the restart still needed. Both fixes are the same shape: synchronize on the observable state rather than on a clock. Poll until the first turn is recorded, kill, then wait for the supervisor's restart to land before standing processes down. A test that races the runtime it is testing reports the race, not the behavior.

A resumed session came back with the right driver context and the wrong world: after a real VM restart the global Tiller.ToolState starts from defaults, so a run that had called put or spend continued against a world that had forgotten it. The existing test could not see this because reset_processes/0 leaves the global ToolState process alive, simulating a restart that keeps something a restart destroys. Ask of any recovery test: what does my teardown leave running that the real failure would have killed? Fix was to resume from snap.tool_state, which after a restart is the only copy.

Four traps in one build, all failing quietly rather than raising. (1) config server: false silently defeats mix phx.server, because Phoenix reads it with Keyword.get_lazy; set it only under PHX_SERVER. (2) DynamicSupervisor's default max_restarts of 3-in-5s, tripped by deliberate kills, took down every resumed session with nothing pointing at the cause; a parallel session hit and fixed the same thing independently, so it is a real trap and not a one-off. (3) :httpc is not on the code path at all without :inets in extra_applications. (4) A tool calling GenServer.call on its own session deadlocks; pass the id through the process dictionary instead.

String.to_atom on a tool name or stop reason the model invented is an atom-table exhaustion vector: the BEAM never garbage-collects atoms, so untrusted strings that become atoms are an unbounded resource leak ending in VM death. Any LLM harness on the BEAM inherits this. The guard belongs at the wire boundary, where the decoder maps known names through a fixed table and keeps everything else a binary, rather than deeper in where the atom has already been interned.

Two Claude sessions independently built the same butterfly lab from the same design doc and drove both to main; one merged first, leaving the other's PR unmergeable and its work to be salvaged as four separate ports. The port only worked cleanly because the pieces happened to be separable, which was luck. open-seed exists to prevent exactly this (scripts/seed task claim is synchronous and exclusive, exit 2 means someone else has it), and we were building tiller without using it. The tiller-as-MCP-client integration is what would make claiming available to both sessions.
